title: A Promise for a Weeping Queen
subtitle: What Krishna swore to Draupadi in the Kamyaka forest
story:
Some sorrows cannot be answered with plans for war. In the Kamyaka forest, while the kinsmen talked of vengeance, Draupadi sat apart and wept.

Her husbands had lost everything at dice — kingdom, wealth, dignity — and were living in exile in the great forest, far from the comforts of their old life. The whole morning the clearing had been full of their friends, come from near and far with hearts fired with wrath against the sons of Dhritarashtra: the Bhojas, the Vrishnis and the Andhakas, the relatives of Panchala, the king of Chedi, the Kaikeya brothers. They had sat in a wide circle around Yudhishthira, and Krishna at their head had vowed that the earth would drink the blood of Duryodhana and Karna, of Dussasana and the wicked Sakuni, and that Yudhishthira would sit on the throne again. But that was talk of battles yet to come, and it is cold comfort to a woman who has already lost. She was the princess of Panchala, the shared wife of the five brothers, and she had tasted enough of the Kauravas' cruelty to know that vows and battles are cheap until they are kept. Her anger had names, and each of them sat safely in Hastinapura while she sat weeping on forest grass.

Krishna saw her tears, and he did not offer her patience or philosophy. Vasudeva spoke to the weeping Draupadi, and his words were a promise laid against the future like a stone.

"O fair lady," he said, "the wives of those with whom thou art angry shall weep even like thee, beholding their husbands dead on the ground, weltering in blood."

Then he went further — much further. "I promise thou shalt once more be the queen of kings! The heavens might fall, or the Himavat might split, the earth might be rent, or the waters of the ocean might dry up, but my words shall never prove futile."

For a moment the forest seemed to hold its breath. It was an odd comfort, to a woman who had been wronged before a court: not "bear it patiently," but "they will weep as you weep now, and you will sit on a throne again." Krishna did not soften the wrong or blur the memory of it. He swore that it would be answered, measure for measure, and he staked the order of nature itself on his word — the heavens might fall, the Himavat split, the earth be rent, the oceans dry up, before that promise would break. And this, the forest knew, was not the language of a man comforting a woman; it was the language of a king giving his word before witnesses.

The weeping Draupadi heard him, and her tears slowed on her face. Those who knew Krishna knew that his word, once given, was firmer than the ground under their feet. Even Arjuna, standing among the allies, said nothing; there was nothing to add to a vow that had made the sky its surety.

In the evening, the talk among the gathered kings turned from grief to plans — of armies and alliances, and of the war that waited at the end of thirteen years. But those who had heard Krishna's words to Draupadi carried something else away with them: the memory of a queen weeping in exile, and the man who had promised her a throne with the fall of heaven as the only price of his failing. She, for her part, began that evening to believe it — because she knew, as everyone in that camp knew, that Krishna had never in his life spoken a word that the world had not, in the end, been forced to keep.
reflection: Krishna does not tell Draupadi to be patient or to forget. He answers grief with a counter-vow, matching the wrong done to her with a future so certain that he stakes the order of nature on it — heaven falling, oceans drying up — before he will let his word fail. Consolation here is not softness; it is the same iron promise that will later be kept on the battlefield.
next_story_tease: Then Krishna turned to Yudhishthira with a confession that had been burning in him since Dwaraka.
hero_scene: The weeping Draupadi seated apart in the forest clearing while Krishna, standing before her, makes his vow with one hand raised — the gathered kings and allies dim behind them, and evening light slanting through the trees.
